title: ML numerics: loss becomes NaN with large logits — softmax overflows; subtract max(x) first
problemSummary: Hand-rolled softmax computed as exp(x)/sum(exp(x)) produces Infinity/Infinity=NaN (JS) or an overflow exception (Python) as soon as any logit exceeds ~709 in float64 (~88 in float32). Symptom: loss is NaN on the very first forward pass, training diverges instantly, and the operator wastes hours blaming the learning rate, the data, or the architecture when the cause is pure floating-point arithmetic.

versions.symptoms: loss = NaN from step 0 or the first confident prediction; model outputs become all-zero or NaN; bug appears after switching a model to raw logits or when predictions get confident; float32 breaks at logits > ~88 while float64 breaks at > ~709
versions.rootCause: IEEE-754 doubles overflow above exp(709.78): exp(1000)=Infinity, and Infinity/Infinity=NaN (or OverflowError in Python math.exp). Softmax is mathematically invariant to shifting ALL logits by a constant, so subtracting max(x) changes nothing mathematically but bounds every exponent argument to <= 0, making overflow impossible.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) z = x - max(x)  2) e = exp(z)  3) softmax = e / sum(e). Never implement softmax without the max shift. In frameworks use the fused op which does this internally: torch.softmax / F.log_softmax, tf.nn.softmax, scipy.special.softmax. Related: never compute cross-entropy as log(softmax(x)) — use the log-sum-exp form (companion record in this library).
versions.environment: Any float stack: PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, NumPy, hand-rolled JS/Python math. Float32 is hit 8x earlier than float64.
versions.applicableVersions: Applies to all versions — IEEE-754 semantics are fixed by the standard
versions.limitations: No exceptions: subtracting the max is mandatory in EVERY hand-rolled softmax, even for "small" logits, because input scale is rarely guaranteed upstream.

title: ML numerics: cross-entropy Infinity or NaN gradients on confident predictions — use log-sum-exp, never log(softmax)
problemSummary: Computing categorical cross-entropy as -log(softmax(x)[y]) underflows to probability exactly 0.0 for confident-but-wrong predictions, so loss = -log(0) = +Infinity and gradients become NaN. Symptom: training runs fine for a while, then explodes the moment the model becomes confident on one class; NaN gradients appear sporadically and "randomly".

versions.symptoms: loss = Infinity on a confident wrong prediction; NaN gradients after some epochs; sporadic NaN that appears only once the model stops being uncertain; the same code trains fine early and breaks later
versions.rootCause: softmax outputs can underflow to exactly 0.0 in floating point (any probability below ~1e-308 in float64, ~1e-45 in float32), and log(0) = -Infinity. The stable identity avoids softmax entirely: CE = logsumexp(x) - x[y], where logsumexp(x) = max(x) + log(sum(exp(x - max(x)))). The max-shift keeps every exp argument <= 0 and the log of the sum stays finite.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) m = max(x)  2) lse = m + log(sum(exp(x[i] - m)))  3) CE = lse - x[y]. In PyTorch use F.cross_entropy on RAW logits (never log_softmax then cross_entropy — double application of log); for binary cross-entropy use BCEWithLogitsLoss, never sigmoid then log. In NumPy/JS use scipy.special.logsumexp / the identity above. Do not add an epsilon — the max shift makes epsilon unnecessary and it only masks bugs.
versions.environment: Any ML stack; critical in float32 training and all hand-rolled loss implementations
versions.applicableVersions: Applies to all versions — IEEE-754 underflow semantics are fixed
versions.limitations: Covers softmax cross-entropy; sigmoid/BCE has the analogous logits rule. Other losses (sparsemax etc.) have their own stable implementations — check before hand-rolling.

title: ML data leakage: fitting scaler/encoder on the full dataset inflates validation metrics — split first, fit on train only
problemSummary: Computing normalization statistics (mean/std/min-max), target encodings, imputation values, or feature selection on the FULL dataset before splitting leaks test information into training. Validation metrics look great; production performance collapses. Symptom: offline metrics "too good to be true" compared to any live or holdout-later evaluation — the classic silent leakage failure.

versions.symptoms: validation metrics suspiciously better than production/live performance; k-fold CV much better than a time-based split of the same data; results degrade the moment someone re-splits the data properly; temporal data normalized with future statistics
versions.rootCause: Test-set values contribute to the very statistics used to transform them, so the transform itself carries information about the test distribution — the test set is normalized toward the training distribution instead of being honestly out-of-sample. With shifted distributions (e.g. time series where later values are larger) every normalized test value is biased by its own contamination.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) Split FIRST — by time for temporal data, by entity (user/company) when rows share an origin; never random-split temporal data. 2) Fit the scaler/encoder/imputer on the TRAIN split only. 3) Transform both train and test with the train-fitted scaler. 4) In sklearn wrap preprocessing + model in a Pipeline so cross-validation refits the scaler inside each fold. 5) Audit existing code: if train-mean equals full-dataset-mean while a test set exists, there is leakage. 6) Same rule for: target encoding, missing-value imputation, feature selection, NLP vocabulary building, and augmentation statistics.
versions.environment: sklearn/pandas pipelines, PyTorch preprocessing, any tabular ML workflow
versions.limitations: Leakage through duplicate rows (same entity in train and test) needs entity-aware splitting, not just statistic hygiene. Leakage through temporal features (e.g. "days since event" computed with future knowledge) must be fixed at feature design time.

title: NN training: immediate NaN loss or dead flat loss in deep ReLU network — wrong weight init scale; use He init std = sqrt(2/fan_in)
problemSummary: Initializing weights with plain random values (std=1, uniform(-1,1)) scales activations by ~fan_in at every layer: a 20-layer net with 64 units explodes activations to ~1e28 (NaN gradients) — or with too-small weights, activations vanish to 0 and the loss never moves at any learning rate. Symptom: immediate NaN in deep nets, or loss pinned at its initialization value while the operator tunes the LR pointlessly.

versions.symptoms: loss = NaN within the first updates of a deep net; loss completely flat from step 0 regardless of learning rate; activation histograms grow/shrink by orders of magnitude with depth; "small nets train, deep nets die"
versions.rootCause: For a linear layer y = Wx with n inputs, Var(y) ~ n * E[w^2] * Var(x). To keep activation variance constant across layers with ReLU (which zeroes half the units), you need E[w^2] = 2/n — i.e. He/Kaiming initialization, std = sqrt(2/fan_in). Naive std=1 weights multiply the second moment by n/2 every layer (64x -> dead by layer 20); tiny weights shrink it toward 0.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) Use He/Kaiming init for ReLU-family activations: normal(std=sqrt(2/fan_in)) — torch.nn.init.kaiming_normal_ (PyTorch default for Conv/Linear since 1.0). 2) Xavier/Glorot (sqrt(1/fan_in) or its uniform variant) for tanh/sigmoid. 3) LeakyReLU uses sqrt(2/(1+alpha^2))/sqrt(fan_in). 4) Sanity check: forward one batch through the UNTRAINED net and print activation std per layer — it should stay within roughly [0.5, 2] of the input std at EVERY depth; if layer-20 is ~0 or ~>1e6, the init is wrong. 5) For very deep nets (>~30 layers) add BatchNorm/LayerNorm as the robust fix.
versions.environment: PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, hand-rolled nets; fully-connected and conv architectures (conv fan_in = kh*kw*in_channels)
versions.applicableVersions: Frameworks default correctly for standard layers — this bites in hand-rolled layers, custom activations, and code ported between frameworks
versions.limitations: Also check the accompanying loss function numerics (softmax/CE records in this library) — NaN can come from either place; the per-layer activation-std print distinguishes them.

title: SQLite migration safety: file-copy the .db before any schema change — a byte-identical copy IS a complete backup
problemSummary: Running prisma db push / migrate / raw ALTER TABLE against the ONLY copy of a SQLite database with no backup, then hitting data loss (--accept-data-loss) or a lock mid-migration, leaves no recovery path. SQLite has no server-side snapshot: the .db file is the entire database, which also makes it the cheapest database in the world to back up — the step everyone skips.

versions.symptoms: schema migration ran with --accept-data-loss and dropped data; database locked / disk I/O error mid-migration corrupts the file; "we lost the dev database"; rollback impossible because no copy existed
versions.rootCause: SQLite stores schema, data, indices and WAL in a single file. A byte-copy of that file taken while no write transaction is open is a complete, restorable database. Migrations mutate that single file in place, so without a pre-copy any mistake is permanent.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) BEFORE any schema change: cp db/<name>.db db/<name>.backup-$(date +%s).db and verify the copy with cmp -s (byte-identical). 2) Prefer additive changes: new nullable column, new table — avoid in-place mutation of existing columns. 3) Add NOT NULL columns WITH a DEFAULT value. 4) Prototype with prisma db push; keep migration history with prisma migrate dev once the schema stabilizes. 5) Test the migration on the BACKUP COPY first, then run it on the real file. 6) For live/WAL-mode databases use sqlite3 <db> ".backup <target>" instead of a raw cp (safe while writers are active).
versions.environment: SQLite + Prisma (this bridge stack: bun run db:push), any SQLite-backed application
versions.limitations: A raw cp is only safe when no writer is active (stop the dev server / run migrations offline). The sqlite3 .backup command is the safe online alternative. WAL sidecar files (-wal, -shm) must be copied together or checkpointed first.

title: ML debugging: network does not learn — overfit 10 samples FIRST (single-batch sanity protocol) before tuning anything
problemSummary: Engineers and AI operators burn hours tuning architecture, optimizers and hyperparameters on networks that have an implementation bug. The highest-ROI FIRST test — can the network memorize a tiny batch? — is skipped, and the session spirals into exactly the overthinking this knowledge library exists to prevent. Failure to overfit a small batch is STRONG EVIDENCE for a mechanical bug, not proof: insufficient steps, too-low LR or (rarely) genuine capacity limits can also fail the test — the protocol below discriminates between them.

versions.symptoms: loss plateaus immediately at its initial value; model predicts the mean/class prior for every input; "tried 5 different architectures and none of them learn"; loss decreases on nothing at any learning rate
versions.rootCause: If a network cannot overfit 10 samples, the bug is mechanical — labels misaligned with inputs, loss applied to the wrong tensor, detach() breaking gradients, wrong loss for the label dtype, preprocessing destroying the signal — NOT capacity or hyperparameters. Overfitting a tiny batch cleanly separates implementation bugs from generalization problems.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) Take ~10 training samples. 2) Train ONLY on them (many epochs) until loss < ~1e-2 or accuracy is 100%. 3) If it cannot: (a) print tensor SHAPES at every boundary; (b) verify labels align with inputs — if data was shuffled, confirm inputs and labels were shuffled TOGETHER; (c) verify the loss receives raw logits + correct label dtype (CrossEntropyLoss wants long/int labels, no softmax applied); (d) run one backward pass and assert every parameter has non-None, non-zero grad; (e) inspect the inputs themselves (print a sample — is the signal actually there?). 4) Only after the tiny batch overfits, scale to full data — if training loss now rises while tiny-batch worked, the problem is data volume/regularization, not code.
versions.environment: Any deep learning framework — the single highest-ROI debugging step in NN work
versions.limitations: For very large models, reduce width or freeze early layers — the point is mechanical correctness, not convergence speed. RL has the analogous sanity: random-agent returns on a trivially small environment before any training.
versions.verificationSummary: not verified yet — run knowledge verify with real checks, or approve on the dashboard

versions.rootCause: The single-batch test is a discriminator between two failure families: (1) mechanical bugs — labels misaligned with inputs, loss applied to the wrong tensor, detach() breaking gradients, wrong loss for the label dtype, preprocessing destroying the signal — the common case; (2) convergence limits — too-few steps, too-low LR, rarely capacity. If the network cannot memorize a few samples even after training longer at a raised LR, family (1) is near-certain. Treating every failure-to-learn as family (2) — tuning hyperparameters against a broken pipeline — is the anti-pattern.
versions.solutionSteps:
1) Take ~10 training samples that SPAN the classes (>= 2 per class). A single-class batch voids the test: a constant predictor then reaches 100% accuracy with zero learning. 2) Disable augmentation / dropout / weight decay for the test and train ONLY on those samples. PASS CRITERIA are scale-relative, never a fixed constant: (a) batch accuracy reaches 100% (classification), or predictions match targets within target scale (regression); (b) loss falls far below its step-0 value and plateaus near the floor a memorizing model can reach — for cross-entropy that floor is ~0 and the step-0 value should be near ln(K) for K classes. A fixed threshold like loss < 1e-2 is NOT a valid criterion: loss scale depends on the loss family and target scale (MSE on targets in the 1000s may never reach 1e-2 even when fully memorized). 3) If the batch will not overfit after training longer at a raised LR, hunt the mechanical bug: (a) print tensor SHAPES at every boundary; (b) verify labels align with inputs — if data was shuffled, confirm inputs and labels were shuffled TOGETHER; (c) verify the loss receives raw logits and the label dtype it expects (e.g. CrossEntropyLoss expects integer class indices and applies softmax internally — doc-verifiable per framework version, not verified here); (d) check GRADIENT HEALTH, not all-non-zero: assert (i) no NaN/Inf grads anywhere and (ii) every layer that should train has at least one non-zero grad. Individual zero grads are NORMAL and expected — dead ReLU units, embedding rows absent from the tiny batch, frozen parameters (requires_grad=False gives .grad = None by design), unused graph branches. Asserting every parameter is non-zero is a false-positive generator, not a health check. (e) print the inputs themselves — is the signal actually present? 4) Only after the tiny batch overfits, scale to full data. If full-data training misbehaves while the tiny batch overfits cleanly, that POINTS TO generalization / regularization / data-pipeline causes (augmentation too strong, LR mismatched to the new batch size, shuffle or scaling bug appearing at scale) rather than a forward/backward bug — confirm by disabling augmentation and re-running before concluding.

Treating every failure-to-learn as family (2) — tuning hyperparameters against a broken pipeline — is the anti-pattern.
versions.solutionSteps:
1) Take ~10 training samples that SPAN the classes (>= 2 per class). A single-class batch voids the test: a constant predictor then reaches 100% accuracy with zero learning. 2) Disable augmentation / dropout / weight decay for the test and train ONLY on those samples. PASS CRITERIA are scale-relative, never a fixed constant: (a) batch accuracy reaches 100% (classification), or predictions match targets within target scale (regression); (b) loss falls far below its step-0 value and plateaus near the floor a memorizing model can reach — for cross-entropy that floor is ~0 and the step-0 value should be near ln(K) for K classes. A fixed threshold like loss < 1e-2 is NOT a valid criterion: loss scale depends on the loss family and target scale (MSE on targets in the 1000s may never reach 1e-2 even when fully memorized). 3) If the batch will not overfit after training longer at a raised LR, hunt the mechanical bug: (a) print tensor SHAPES at every boundary; (b) verify labels align with inputs — if data was shuffled, confirm inputs and labels were shuffled TOGETHER; (c) verify the loss receives raw logits and the label dtype it expects (e.g. CrossEntropyLoss expects integer class indices and applies softmax internally — doc-verifiable per framework version, not verified here); (d) check GRADIENT HEALTH, not all-non-zero: assert (i) no NaN/Inf grads anywhere and (ii) every layer that should train has at least one non-zero grad. Individual zero grads are NORMAL and expected — dead ReLU units, embedding rows absent from the tiny batch, frozen parameters (requires_grad=False gives .grad = None by design), unused graph branches. Asserting every parameter is non-zero is a false-positive generator, not a health check. (e) print the inputs themselves — is the signal actually present? 4) Only after the tiny batch overfits, scale to full data. If full-data training misbehaves while the tiny batch overfits cleanly, that POINTS TO generalization / regularization / data-pipeline causes (augmentation too strong, LR mismatched to the new batch size, shuffle or scaling bug appearing at scale) rather than a forward/backward bug — confirm by disabling augmentation and re-running before concluding.

C2 experimental (python3): a constant predictor scores 100% accuracy on a single-class batch but only ~1/K on a class-spanning batch — validates the class-spanning requirement. C3 doc-based (NOT yet inspected): label-dtype and internal-softmax expectations of the loss actually used, against that framework version's official docs. C4 experimental (requires a DL framework; NOT available on this machine — candidate env: a torch/tf sandbox): run this protocol on a known-correct small network (must PASS) and on a label-shuffled copy (must FAIL) — validates the discriminating power of the test itself.

versions.limitations: Failure to overfit a tiny batch is strong evidence of a mechanical bug, not proof — rule out too-few steps, too-low LR and (rarely) capacity by training longer and wider first. Very large models: reduce width or freeze early layers — the point is mechanical correctness, not convergence speed. RL analogue: random-agent returns on a trivially small environment before any training. Gradient checks verify FLOW, not mathematical correctness — a wrong-but-flowing loss passes them. title: ML triage: read the loss curve before changing anything — each shape narrows to a SHORT CANDIDATE LIST that must be confirmed by a check; a shape alone is never a diagnosis
problemSummary: When training misbehaves, operators jump between speculative fixes (shotgun debugging) instead of reading the loss curve. A curve SHAPE narrows the cause to a small candidate set — it is a CLUE, not a verdict: the same shape is produced by several distinct causes, and each candidate must be confirmed or eliminated by its listed check before you act on it. This record is the triage table: match the shape, run the cheapest discriminating checks, confirm, then fix.

versions.symptoms: loss = NaN early; loss flat from step 0; loss explodes upward after a period of progress; train loss falls while validation loss rises; both losses flatten at a mediocre value
versions.rootCause: Each loss-curve shape has a well-defined, small cause set — the shape is diagnostic information, not noise.
versions.solutionSteps: NaN/Inf EARLY -> learning rate too high (divide by 10), numerical instability in loss/softmax (see the softmax and log-sum-exp records in this library), or inf/nan already present in the input data. FLAT FROM STEP 0 -> LR too low; dead ReLUs (print per-layer activation stats); loss/label mismatch (regression loss on classification labels); or broken graph (detached tensors, optimizer.step() never called). EXPLODES AFTER N GOOD STEPS -> gradient explosion (clip grad norm); LR schedule stepping too aggressively; batch size shrank and per-step noise grew. TRAIN down, VAL up -> overfitting — respond in ROI order: more/augmented data, dropout, weight decay, early stopping (architecture changes LAST). BOTH FLAT AT MEDIOCRE VALUE -> labels nearly constant (class imbalance — check the majority baseline) or inputs uninformative (feature pipeline broken; print samples). When the shape alone is ambiguous, log per-layer activation AND gradient norms and look for the layer where they hit 0 or blow up.
versions.environment: All supervised training loops, any framework
versions.limitations: Curve shapes interact with LR schedules — always do the first diagnosis at a constant LR, then re-introduce warmup/decay.

versions.rootCause: A loss-curve shape is diagnostic evidence that raises the probability of a small set of candidate causes; it is never sufficient by itself for a root-cause conclusion. Example: a flat loss can mean not-learning (value at chance level), already-solved (value near zero), or constant labels (value at the class-prior floor) — the loss VALUE relative to the analytic baseline disambiguates what the shape alone cannot. The method: match shape, get the candidate list, run the cheapest discriminating check first, and only treat a cause as established when its check confirms it.
versions.solutionSteps:
STEP 0 for every flat or plateaued curve: compare the loss VALUE to the analytic baseline. K-class cross-entropy constant-predictor floor = ln(K) (ln 2 = 0.6931 binary; ln 10 = 2.3026 for 10 classes); majority-class floor = class-prior entropy; regression floor = mean-predictor MSE. Flat AT baseline = not learning; flat NEAR ZERO = likely already fit (check a metric, not loss); flat BELOW baseline at a mediocre value = partial learning. SHAPES -> CANDIDATES (confirm before acting): NaN/Inf EARLY -> (a) inf/nan already in the input batch — print per-feature min/max, cheapest check; (b) numeric fault in the loss itself — log(0), softmax overflow (see the log-sum-exp record); (c) LR too high — grad norms at the last healthy step: exploding norms support it, sane norms point back to (a)/(b). Dividing LR by 10 is a MITIGATION to stop the bleeding, not a diagnosis. FLAT FROM STEP 0 -> (a) baseline comparison above; (b) optimizer not stepping or LR not loaded (loss would not even drift — verify optimizer.step() is called and the LR actually in use); (c) loss/label mismatch (regression loss on class labels); (d) broken graph (detached tensors); (e) dead ReLUs — per-layer activation stats: SOME dead units are normal, an ALL-dead layer is not. EXPLODES AFTER N GOOD STEPS -> (a) a single poisoned batch — reproduce with a fixed seed / fixed batch order; if the explosion moves with the shuffle, it is data; (b) gradient explosion — log per-step grad norms; a growing trend confirms; (c) LR schedule stepping too far — inspect the actual LR value at the divergence step. Clipping is an immediate stabilizer; find WHY norms grew (init, LR, loss reduction) before calling it fixed. TRAIN DOWN, VAL UP -> overfitting is the LEADING candidate, not the only one; confirm alternatives first: (a) eval-pipeline parity — same preprocessing, no train-only augmentation at eval; (b) train/val distribution shift — compare label and feature distributions. If confirmed as overfitting, respond in ROI order: more or augmented data, dropout, weight decay, early stopping — architecture changes LAST. BOTH FLAT AT MEDIOCRE VALUE -> (a) labels near-constant — compute the majority-class baseline accuracy; if your metric matches it, the model learned only the prior; (b) inputs uninformative — print samples and audit the feature pipeline; (c) LR too low or capacity too small — briefly raise LR 10x: if the loss finally moves, it was LR. When the shape alone is ambiguous: log per-layer activation AND gradient norms; look for the layer where they hit zero or blow up.

title: Database performance: N+1 queries — latency grows with row count; MEASURE query count first, then batch reads (Prisma include / WHERE IN). SQLite 'database is locked' is a separate write-transaction problem
problemSummary: List endpoints that run 1 query for the rows plus N lazy queries for each row relation become O(N) round-trips: 100 rows can mean 101 queries. Symptom: page latency grows linearly with row count — fast locally, slow with real data. SEPARATE failure mode, frequently confused with it: SQLite 'database is locked' errors — those come from concurrent or long-held WRITE transactions, not from read-side N+1; the two need different fixes (see rootCause).

versions.symptoms: endpoint latency scales with the number of rows returned; query log shows the same query repeated dozens of times per request; SQLite "database is locked" under light concurrency; page loads fine with 10 rows and crawls at 1000
versions.rootCause: Accessing a relation inside a loop triggers one lazy query per row. The database can do this work in a single join or a single keyed batch — the ORM just needs to be asked. Each extra round-trip also holds a SQLite lock longer, compounding contention.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) MEASURE FIRST: enable query logging (Prisma: new PrismaClient({ log: ["query"] })) and count queries per request — more than ~3 for a list view means investigate. 2) Replace loop-accessed relations with include: db.post.findMany({ include: { author: true } }) — one join instead of N queries. 3) For key lists: db.user.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } }) then group in memory. 4) GraphQL servers: DataLoader coalesces same-tick lookups. 5) VERIFY the fix: query count per request must be CONSTANT regardless of row count. 6) If include over-fetches, shape it with select; if you need >2 levels of nested include, suspect a denormalization need rather than a query-pattern problem.
versions.environment: Prisma + SQLite/Postgres (this bridge stack), ORMs generally, GraphQL/REST list endpoints
versions.limitations: include on very large relations can over-fetch — use select to shape payloads. Deep nested includes (>2 levels) usually indicate the schema should be denormalized, not that the query pattern is wrong.

versions.symptoms: endpoint latency scales with the number of rows returned; query log shows the same query repeated dozens of times per request; page loads fine with 10 rows and crawls at 1000. versions.rootCause: Accessing a relation inside a loop triggers one lazy query per row; the work can be fetched in a bounded number of round-trips if the ORM is asked in one call. The exact mechanism (a JOIN vs a constant number of batched queries) DEPENDS on the ORM, its version, the provider (SQLite/Postgres) and the relation shape — do not assume it; measure it with query logging. SQLite locking, corrected: N+1 READS cause latency, not lock errors. In SQLite's rollback-journal model a write transaction holds RESERVED and takes the database lock at commit, blocking other WRITERS; WAL mode allows readers during a write. 'database is locked' therefore indicates concurrent or long-held writes (or a missing busy timeout). This locking explanation is prior knowledge REQUIRING doc + experimental verification before this record is promoted (see plan).
versions.solutionSteps:
1) MEASURE FIRST: enable query logging (Prisma: new PrismaClient({ log: ['query'] })) and COUNT queries per request at TWO row counts (e.g. 10 and 100). N+1 shows as the count growing with rows; the goal is a count CONSTANT w.r.t. row count. 2) Replace loop-accessed relations with one batched read: db.post.findMany({ include: { author: true } }). CAUTION: 'include = one JOIN' is NOT guaranteed — relation loading may compile to a JOIN or to a small number of batched queries depending on ORM version, provider and relation shape. The verifiable requirement is the CONSTANT QUERY COUNT measured in step 1, not a presumed SQL shape. 3) Key lists: db.user.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } }) then group in memory. 4) GraphQL servers: DataLoader coalesces same-tick lookups. 5) VERIFY the fix: recount queries at both row counts — constant count with growing rows = fixed; anything else is not. 6) Over-fetching: shape with select. Nesting depth of ANY level is a COST signal to examine (query complexity, payload size); the response ladder in order of preference: shape with select -> split into separate queries -> push aggregation into the DB (groupBy / raw SQL) -> ONLY for a measured, reproducible hot path: denormalize, accepting an explicit consistency trade-off. There is NO depth threshold that by itself proves denormalization is required. 7) SQLite lock errors are NOT fixed by batching reads. Check for: concurrent writers, long-running or interactive write transactions, missing busy timeout. Candidate mitigations to verify on your stack: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; busy_timeout; keeping write transactions short.

title: AI-operator self-correction: verify an API exists in the INSTALLED project before using it — hallucinated APIs are a recurrent, high-severity agent failure mode
problemSummary: LLM agents (including the operator writing this) confidently use APIs from training memory: functions that do not exist in the installed version, options added in later releases, or methods from a different library with the same name. The code looks plausible and fails at runtime with 'x.y is not a function'. This is a RECURRENT, high-severity failure mode of agent-written code and one of the cheapest to prevent. (Frequency ranking is unquantified — no dataset ranks agent bug sources, so v1's '#1' claim is retracted.)

versions.symptoms: TypeError: x.y is not a function; "property does not exist on type"; an option is silently ignored instead of changing behavior; "works in the docs" but not in this project — version drift
versions.rootCause: Model memory blends versions, libraries and APIs into plausible-looking calls. The project node_modules, @types and package.json are ground truth; memory is only a prior, never evidence. Treating memory as evidence produces code that was never valid for THIS project.

Cost: seconds per check, versus hours of runtime debugging.

title: AI-operator self-correction: minimal surgical edits, one change per cycle, revert before the next attempt — the antidote to overthinking
problemSummary: When an error resists the first fix, LLM agents escalate: rewriting whole files, changing many things at once, stacking speculative fixes on top of failed ones. This destroys working state, introduces new bugs, and hides which change mattered — the canonical overthinking failure mode this knowledge library exists to break.

versions.symptoms: a small bug fix turned into a 300-line diff; the error message changed but the root cause was never addressed; "fixed A, broke B"; a file was rewritten and now diverges from what git and the tests know; two failed fixes stacked into unknown state
versions.rootCause: Multiple simultaneous changes make cause and effect unattributable, and rewrites discard code that encoded working knowledge. Debugging is a search problem: every iteration must be ONE attributable change with a measured result. Stacking fixes on failures explores the wrong branch of the search tree while corrupting the starting point.
versions.solutionSteps: 1) Make the smallest edit that plausibly addresses the CAUSE (anchored edit, not file rewrite). 2) After a failed attempt, REVERT it before trying the next — never stack fixes on a failed one. 3) Change ONE variable at a time and re-run the exact failing check after each change. 4) If two attempts fail: STOP. Re-read the ACTUAL error text (not the assumed one), reduce it to a minimal reproduction, and re-approach from the last known-green state (git checkout/restore the file). 5) Re-read the file after editing to confirm the edit landed as intended. 6) Reserve full rewrites for genuinely unsalvageable files — and require evidence (two failed surgical attempts) before claiming that.

versions.solutionSteps:
1) Make the smallest edit that plausibly addresses the CAUSE (anchored edit, not file rewrite). 2) ONE change per cycle; re-run the exact failing check after each change — that result is the only progress signal. 3) SELECTIVE, SAFE ROLLBACK — never blanket restores: BEFORE the first edit, capture the pre-edit content of ONLY the file(s) you are about to touch (bridge read_file, or git diff to enumerate hunks). On a failed attempt, restore exactly what you changed: git restore -p (choose your hunks), a path-limited stash (git stash push -- <paths>), or re-apply the captured pre-edit content. NEVER run repo-wide git checkout . / git reset --hard — they destroy the user's unrelated uncommitted work. If the file had PRE-EXISTING uncommitted changes, prefer restoring just your hunks over any file-level restore. CONFIRM the rollback: re-run the exact failing check — the ORIGINAL error must reproduce; that is your known-green marker. 4) CONTINUATION CRITERIA — there is no fixed attempt count. Continue surgical attempts while: (a) each attempt tests a NEW hypothesis informed by the actual error text of the previous failure; (b) the diff stays anchored at the failure site; (c) the error is changing or moving (progress signal). STOP and surface the situation to the user when: attempts repeat the same hypothesis with no new information; the diff keeps growing past the causal site; or you can no longer attribute which change did what. 5) Re-read the file after editing to confirm the edit landed as intended. 6) Re-read the ACTUAL error text (not the assumed one) before each next attempt; reduce to a minimal reproduction when the system resists. 7) Reserve full-file rewrites for files whose STRUCTURE is itself the demonstrated cause — not merely because surgical attempts failed: require structural evidence or exhausted-information signals from step 4, and surface the rewrite decision to the user whenever the blast radius is non-trivial.
